newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Bosnian Moslem guard set prisoner alight -witness.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Moslem guard set prisoner alight -witness.

text.p: Hitching up his trouser leg to display old scars, a Serb survivor of the Celebici prison camp in Bosnia told a U.N. war crimes tribunal on Wednesday how he was doused in petrol and set alight by a camp guard.

The first Celebici inmate to take the witness stand, 63-year-old Mirko Babic told the tribunal that Esad Landzo, one of the Moslem guards at the camp facing the tribunal, had summoned him on several occasions, beating and torturing him.

Landzo, 24, is charged along with fellow Moslems Hazim Delic and Zejnil Delalic with war crimes allegedly committed at the camp. A fourth accused, Bosnian Croat Zdravko "Pavo" Mucic, 41, was the camp's commander. All four deny the charges.

The trial, the third to be heard by the war crimes tribunal for former Yugoslavia since it was established in 1993, is the first group trial and also the first to focus on alleged Moslem atrocities in the 3-1/2 year Bosnian conflict.

Speaking so fast he was repeatedly asked to slow down by court interpreters, Babic recounted a string of incidents during his four-month stay at the camp in central Bosnia five years ago when inmates were beaten, tortured and sometimes killed.
"One time around the 20th July 1992...he (Landzo) set fire to my leg," Babic told the court.
"Landzo took me to the same spot where I was beaten before and ordered me to lie down and uncover my legs," Babic said.

"He held a bottle in his hand...and when he poured it on my legs I could smell it was gasoline. I saw the flame, it was very painful." Afterwards the leg blistered and yellow pus poured from it, he said.

Babic, who weighed just 39 kg (86 lb) on his release, said conditions at the overcrowded camp had been intolerable. He and 250 other inmates were housed in a hangar where they sat on the bare concrete floor.

"It was very dirty. There was a bucket behind the door for toilet purposes...there were five spoons for 250 of us, we ate in turns," Babic recalled. "One time in July we were given nothing to eat for 56 hours."

Babic, who said he knew Delic personally and close relatives of Landzo before the war as they had all worked for the same firm, said on another occasion he had been beaten unconscious by Delic, the camp's deputy commander, Landzo and another man.
But he said other prisoners had been worse treated.
One prisoner's hands were tied behind his back before he was beaten and led away, Babic said.
"He was taken out of the hangar and he did not come back," he said, adding he had heard later the man had died.
"The second victim was some time around June 15... around 12 noon Hazim Delic and Esad Landzo told (him) to get up (saying) 'you have killed 42 Moslems and we will kill you'," Babic said.
He said the man had been led out of the hangar and beaten several times. On the last occasion they had thrown him back "and he had something fixed onto his forehead," Babic said.
"He was dead, and the next morning they took him away."
The prosecution alleges that in one particularly grisly incident a camp inmate was murdered by nailing a Moslem political badge to his forehead.
Landzo, shaven-headed and wearing a charcoal grey cardigan, shirt and tie, scribbled notes throughout the testimony.
The other three defendants appeared relaxed, swapping occasional whispered comments, but conferred intensively with their respective counsels when the court recessed.
Most of the 74 men so far charged by the tribunal are Serbs. Only seven suspects are actually in its custody.

Tribunal judges are expected later this month to announce their verdict in the six-month trial of Bosnian Serb Dusan Tadic, accused of killing, raping and torturing Moslems in northwest Bosnia in 1992.

Last November Croat Drazen Erdemovic was given a 10-year jail sentence after pleading guilty to taking part in a Serb massacre of over 1,200 unarmed Moslems in Srebrenica in 1995. He is appealing against the sentence.
